title: Gate-based emulation of boson sampling using photonic qubits
authors: Aastha P. Zalone, S. P. Dinesh, C. M. Chandrashekar
abstract: Boson sampling arising from multiphoton interference in linear-optical networks is a prominent non-universal model for quantum computation. Here, by encoding the multi-qubit state to bosonic Fock state, we present a scalable quantum-circuit framework for simulating boson sampling on a universal quantum computing platform. Beginning with balanced beam-splitter transformations on the single- and two-photon sectors, we derive equivalent quantum-circuit implementations and unify them within a common Hilbert-space representation using an ancilla-assisted encoding. This construction is then generalized to arbitrary interferometers by replacing each optical beam splitter with a repeating quantum-circuit unit that selectively acts only within the relevant local interference subspace, requiring $N+1$ qubits for a two-photon $N$-mode interferometer and a linear-overhead subspace-identification procedure. Using this framework, gate-based quantum circuit for a four-mode boson-sampling circuit is developed and experimentally implemented on a four-qubit gate-based photonic qubit system. The qubit framework for emulating boson sampling of $n-$photons in $m-$mode will be useful to solve a broad class of sampling complexity problem on a gate-based quantum computers.
summary: This paper presents a comprehensive method to simulate boson sampling, a key problem in quantum computation, using only universal gate-based photonic qubits. The authors overcome the fundamental mismatch between bosonic Fock states and qubit representations by developing an ancilla-assisted encoding scheme. This allows for the systematic construction of circuits representing arbitrary linear optical interferometers.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing a scalable quantum-circuit framework to simulate boson sampling, which arises from multiphoton interference in linear optics, on universal gate-based quantum computers.
main_result: The authors successfully translate the Fock-space dynamics of bosonic interferometers into an equivalent, systematic sequence of elementary qubit gates, demonstrated for a four-mode system.
method: They derive circuit implementations by encoding multi-qubit bosonic states onto qubits and generalizing beam splitter transformations using repeating quantum-circuit units acting within specific local interference subspaces.
model_or_system: The model is boson sampling realized via linear-optical interferometers. The simulation maps the physics from the natural Fock basis to a universal qubit computational basis, requiring an ancilla-assisted encoding for generalization.
key_observables: Transition probabilities $P(\mathbf{n} 	o \mathbf{s})$ and the permanent of submatrices of the interferometer unitary ($	ext{Perm}(U_{\mathbf{s},\mathbf{n}})$).
important_parameters: The required qubit count scales linearly with the number of modes ($N+1$ qubits for $N$ modes in some contexts); the complexity is related to the permanent calculation.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that a systematic mapping exists to represent all linear-optical transformations using standard quantum gates, even when bridging the gap between Fock and qubit bases.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the circuit representation of beam splitters in single-photon, two-photon, and unified Hilbert spaces. A schematic shows the structure of an $N$-mode interferometer built from these repeating units.
paper_structure: The paper progresses by first analyzing the fundamental building block (beam splitter) for low photon numbers (single/two-photon sectors), unifying this into a general circuit unit, and finally generalizing this unit to construct arbitrary multi-mode interferometers using scalable encoding schemes.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, algorithmic blueprint for simulating complex bosonic quantum phenomena—which are often difficult to model classically due to the permanent calculation—on near-term gate-based hardware architectures.

figures.caption: FIG. 5: Schematic representation of the four-mode linear optical interferometer composed of three balanced beam splitters. The first interferometric stage consists of beam splitters B12 and B34 acting on modes (1, 2) and (3, 4), respectively, producing the intermediate state |ψ1⟩. The second stage comprises beam splitter B23 acting on the central modes (2, 3), resulting in the final output state |ψ2⟩.

FIG. 6: Generalized input-independent quantum circuit corresponding to the four-mode two-photon interferometer. Each optical beam splitter is replaced by the encoded two-photon beam-splitter unit derived in Sec. IV. Ancilla-assisted spectator-mode identification activates the local transformation only within the corresponding two-photon interference subspace. The circuit reproduces the complete four-mode evolution for all physical input states in the encoded Hilbert space.

FIG. 7: Optimized quantum circuits corresponding to the six input states of the four-mode interferometer. Qubits q0, q1, and q3 represent path qubits, whereas q2 represents the polarization qubit. Here, H and X denote the Hadamard and Pauli-X gates, respectively.

FIG. 8: Schematic of the experimental setup for heralded single-photon generation. The remaining optical arrangement constitutes a standard type-II Sagnac interferometer. λ/2, half-wave plates; λ/4, quarter-wave plates; LP, linear polarizer; L, lens of focal length 20 cm; M1–M5, mirrors; D-PBS, dual-wavelength polarizing beam splitter; DM, dichroic mirror; PPKTP, periodically poled potassium titanyl phosphate crystal; FC, fibre couplers; SPCM, single-photon counting modules. The blue thick line indicates the 405 nm pump laser, while the red lines indicate the down-converted photons at 810 nm.

FIG. 9: Three-layered balanced beam-splitter network mapping a single photon in eight spatial modes onto the computational basis states |000⟩–|111⟩of three path-encoded qubits. Each binary label records the sequence of path choices through the network.
